items.requirement: The service must keep a record of each company's drones, and each drone must belong to exactly one company.

For each drone, the service must record its model and manufacturer, how much it can carry, how far it can fly on a full battery, which sensors it carries, which charging connector it uses, and its home site.
A fleet technician must be able to add a new drone to their own company's fleet.
A fleet technician must be able to retire a drone of their own company's fleet.
A fleet technician must be able to take a drone of their own company out of service for repair.
A fleet technician must be able to put a drone of their own company back into service after repair.
The service must not allow a flight to be signed off with a drone that is out of service or retired.

The service must keep, for each drone, a dated history of when it was added, taken out of service for repair, put back into service, and retired. This lets the company show a regulator how the drone has been looked after.
The service must keep a drone's history after the drone has been retired.
The service must keep a record of each company's sites, and each site must belong to exactly one company.
A fleet technician must be able to set up a charging pad at one of their own company's sites. Each site must be able to hold at least a few dozen charging pads.
A fleet technician must be able to send one of their own company's drones to charge at one of their own company's charging pads.
The service must refuse to send a drone to charge at a charging pad that belongs to another company.
The service must refuse to send a drone to charge at a charging pad whose connector does not match the drone's charging connector.
The service must not assign one charging pad to two drones at the same time, even when two people try to assign it at the same moment.
A dispatcher must be able to plan a flight for a job by choosing which of their company's drones flies it and which way it flies through the corridor network.
The service must never choose a drone or a way for a flight on its own. The drone and the way of every flight must be the ones the dispatcher chose.
A flight must not be allowed to leave until a dispatcher has signed it off.
The service must record which dispatcher signed off each flight and when, because that dispatcher is the licensed person responsible for it.
When asked by a dispatcher, the service must list which of the dispatcher's company's drones could get to where a job starts. It must not pick one of them for the dispatcher.
When several dispatchers plan at the same time, the service must not let the same drone be committed to two flights that overlap in time.
When a dispatcher's plan cannot go ahead because another dispatcher has already taken the drone or charging pad, the service must tell that dispatcher.
A dispatcher must be able to call off a flight, both before it leaves and while it is flying.
When a dispatcher signs off a flight whose way passes through a closed corridor or zone, the service must warn the dispatcher before the sign-off is completed.
Users of one company must not be able to see or change another company's drones, charging pads, sites, jobs, flights or problems.
The service must never lend one company's charging pad to another company's drone.
The airspace desk must be able to create, change and remove the flight corridors between sites.
The airspace desk must be able to create, change and remove the zones that group corridors.
The airspace desk must be able to enter closures announced by the authorities, saying which corridors or zones are closed.
The airspace picture (corridors, zones and closures) must be the same for every company, and users of every company must be able to see it.
The airspace desk must not be able to see any single company's drones, sites, jobs, flights or problems.

When a closure is entered, the service must show the airspace desk how much disruption it caused across customers. For example, it could show the number of signed-off flights whose way passes through the closed corridors or zones.
The service must show the disruption from a closure only as totals across all customers. It must not break the totals down by company or show which company's flights were affected.

The service must not lose any record of drones, charging pads, sites, flights, sign-offs, closures or histories when it is restarted for an update or when it crashes. This includes flights that are in the air at that moment.
After a restart or crash, the service must be working again within a few minutes.
When a report from a drone arrives more than once, the service must treat it as one report.
When a drone's reports arrive late or out of order, the service must not let an older report overwrite information from a newer one.
For each drone, the service must show when its most recent report was received, so that users can see when reports have stopped arriving.
When an instruction to a drone or to charging equipment gets through more than once, it must have the same effect as if it had got through once.
When the sender cannot tell whether an instruction to a drone or to charging equipment arrived, the service must allow the instruction to be sent again without causing a second, different effect.
